selection.input: facingDeg, screen space, 0 = +x right, 90 = +y down toward the camera
selection.note: The four quadrants give four orientations per pose. Mirroring reads as a turn because the drawn views already have the head and body angled off-axis.

twoView.layout: 1536 x 1024 RGBA, front left, back right, one pose per file

fourView.layout: 1536 x 1024 RGBA, left to right: stand front, stand back, sit front, sit back
fourView.note: One sheet is the complete source for all eight states. Preferred layout for new characters. Cuts are measured from the alpha channel, not from the RGB: brother-01 view 3 and view 4 actually touch, joined across five rows at x=1156, so its third cut is the narrowest waist rather than a gap.

columnCuts.note: informational only; splitting is by component

fourView.splitting: By alpha connected component, not by column. brother-01 view 3 and view 4 overlap horizontally — one boy's backpack reaches past the other's left edge — so any vertical cut slices a figure. Erode to break the bridge, label, then grow each label back over the full alpha so each view carries only its own figure.

scale.note: dog-01 is a shetland sheepdog; 0.55 m is head-up standing height, approximate.
scale.seatedNote: A seated adult is about 1.25 m against 1.65 m standing. This cannot be measured off the art: the stand and sit sheets are each framed to fill their own canvas, so their pixel heights share no scale. Every pose height has to be set explicitly.

unused.boy-01-shorts-stand.png: kept but not expected to be used; boy-01 has a second outfit that is already covered

alpha.note: Every sheet is RGBA with a transparent background — all 22 have fully transparent borders. There is no backdrop to remove. Anything that looks like a black vignette or a warm gradient is the RGB left under transparent pixels, visible only when a viewer flattens the image onto black. Read the alpha channel; never key the RGB.

legibility.note: Below about 24 world units a figure loses its distinguishing detail: a seated child at table-far is 20 units, roughly 13 x 20 px, and a backpack becomes four blue pixels. Anchors near the horizon are small — cafe-counter 18.5, table-far 20 to 22, counter stools 22 to 25 for a child — while table-near gives 29 to 35 and the bench 36 to 40. Put the characters whose detail matters near the camera.

seatedAnchoring.method: hip on the painted seat top; size from the ramp and sitting height
seatedAnchoring.note: The seat tops in anchors.json are painted by the owner onto the scene, so a chair's height and its floor line are read rather than guessed. A seated sprite puts its hip on that surface. Size does NOT come from the seat's painted width: that quad lies on the ground plane and the projection stretches it to roughly 1.8x the chair's real width, while a sitter's shoulders stand upright and get no such stretch, so matching a body to its seat's width made a 1.65 m man read 2.4 m tall. A sitter covers the middle of the seat and leaves its front edge showing, which is what a chair looks like from this angle. The feet land wherever the drawing puts them and are not corrected: rising 0.42 m onto the seat and stepping 0.45 m back off the chair reach nearly the same screen row here.

sittingHeightMetres._note: Seat surface to the top of the head. Showa-era Japanese sitting height (zakou) runs about 0.90 m for an adult man and 0.84 m for an adult woman, a little less with age. One figure for every adult made the office worker read short next to the women on the counter, which is what the owner saw. Children scale with stature off the child figure.

seatedAnchoring.sittingHeightNote: hip to top of head, which is anatomically stable across poses

hipFraction._note: measured by eye off the art, fraction of sprite height above its bottom edge; adjust if a character sits wrong

kneeFraction._note: read off the art: (x from left, y from bottom) as fractions of the sprite box

hipFractionBack._note: back views put the hip much lower in the sprite than front views do, because the legs are hidden behind the body; measured off the art

seatCoverage._note: multiplier on the ramp-derived seated height, per character; 1.0 is the anatomical size

seatedAnchoring.sitMarksNote: Measured off the owner-marked sheets in marks/, by read-marks.py. Fractions of sprite height above the sprite bottom; hipX/kneeX are fractions of sprite width from its left. hip is where the buttocks meet the seat and is the anchor; knee is the check that the sitter is not floating off the front of the chair. Characters with no sheet yet fall back to hipFraction, which is eyeballed.
seatedAnchoring.wholeOnSeatNote: The owner's call: these two are small enough to sit entirely on the painted seat, feet and all, so they need no hip alignment. Their sprite bottom goes on the seat's front edge and they centre on it. Everyone else is anchored by the marked buttock line, because their feet reach past the front of the chair and the two cannot both be satisfied.
seatedAnchoring.dropUnitsNote: A flat downward nudge on every placed character, seated and standing, in world units. The owner's call, made by eye. 3 units is 6 px in the 1280x720 preview and 12 px against the 2560x1440 background. It was 6, which pushed the three counter stools' sitters off their painted seat tops - those tops are only 5 units deep. A knob, not a measurement.
seatedAnchoring.sizeScaleNote: A flat multiplier on every character's height, on top of the ramp and sitting height. The owner's call: the anatomically correct sizes read too small against this furniture, which is drawn larger than a strict ground-plane projection would give. Seated sprites grow around their buttock line, so the hip stays on the seat and the head and feet move outward. A knob, not a measurement.

drawnFacing._note: Which way a sheet is drawn facing, per pose. Mirroring assumes the art faces screen right and flips it when the character should look left; a sheet drawn facing left needs the opposite. brother-01 is drawn facing left in both poses - his backpack is on the right-hand side of his front sheet, and a backpack is worn on the back.

poseView._note: Force a character to a particular sheet regardless of which way the seat faces. brother-01 is the owner's call: the bench looks out over the open ground, which is a back view, but he should be seen from the front looking left.
